description:
FILED s470bs (Opus) as the second measured residue of #1031 (the first is
#1234).

t/op/filetest.t builds a BLESSED IO ref and asserts, per operator, whether the
`""` handler ran:

    open my $io, "<", "TEST";  $io = *{$io}{IO};  bless $io, "OverString";
    â¦
    # IO refs always get string overload called. This might be a bug.
    $op eq "t" || $op eq "T" || $op eq "B"  and ($exp,$is) = (1,"is");
    $over = 0;  eval "-$op \$io";
    is( $over, $exp, "string overload $is called for -$op on IO");

So for 24 of the 27 operators the handler must NOT run (the IO ref is a
handle), and for `-t`, `-T`, `-B` it MUST.

PCL answers "not called" for all 27, so 24 rows pass and 4 fail (the fourth is
`-l`, whose GLOB-row sibling s470bs fixed; the IO row for `-l` also expects the
handler).  Measured on the s470bs tree: the file's remaining
"string overload is called for -X on IO" failures are exactly 4.

WHY PCL CANNOT ANSWER IT TODAY: `*{$fh}{IO}` and a lexical handle are THE SAME
REPRESENTATION here â a p-box whose payload is a CL stream (s470bs made
`p-glob-slot`'s IO arm return exactly that, which is what fixed #1047's other
half).  perl has two distinct SV types (a GLOB and an IO), and this rule keys
on which one it is.  Answering it needs an IO-ref representation distinct from
a lexical handle box, i.e. a box-model change â not a filetest change.

NOT WORTH IT ON ITS OWN (4 rows, and perl's own test file calls the behaviour
"might be a bug").  Filed so the residue is counted rather than rediscovered,
and so that anyone who DOES give IO refs their own representation knows these
4 rows are waiting for it.
subject: `-t`, `-T` and `-B` on an IO REF run its `""` overload in perl ("IO refs always get string overload called.  This might be a bug." â t/op/filetest.t's own words); PCL cannot distinguish an IO ref from a lexical handle, because both are a box holding a stream.  4 rows.
